prompt.context: Your client is a medical glove manufacturer that sells directly to hospitals in two segments. The first segment is exam gloves, which are single gloves that come in Kleenex boxes. They are disposable and made of latex. The second segment is surgeon gloves, which are used in operating rooms. They come in pairs and they must be of high quality and sterile. The client has come to you because its profit and revenue growth has been slower than that of the competition. They want to know how they can fix this and, in general, how they can improve shareholder value.
prompt.question: How can the client fix its slower-than-competition profit and revenue growth, and in general how can it improve shareholder value?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's overall growth rate?
How many competitors are in the exam glove segment?
clarifying_info.a: 15-20 competitors. Client is market leader with 30% market share; Company A has 20%, Company B has 10%; 15 smaller players (mostly new entrants) hold the rest.

clarifying_info.q: What is happening to prices and margins in the exam glove segment?
clarifying_info.a: Price has been falling somewhat; margins are being squeezed. The segment is growing at 7-8%.

clarifying_info.q: Where is exam glove growth coming from?
clarifying_info.a: New customer segments outside hospitals, such as police departments and fire departments, driven by increased fears of HIV and other diseases and new safety standards.

clarifying_info.q: How many competitors are in the surgical glove segment?
clarifying_info.a: 3 players: client holds 50% market share, Company B holds 30% (same Company B as in exam gloves), Company C holds 20% (does not sell exam gloves).

clarifying_info.q: What is growth like in the surgical glove segment?
clarifying_info.a: 2% growth; prices are stable. Both Company B and Company C are growing faster than the client.

clarifying_info.q: What do surgeons need in terms of gloves?
clarifying_info.a: Not all surgeons have the same needs. For example, some (e.g. bone surgeons) need thicker gloves than what is currently available, so they use 3-4 pairs stacked on top of each other.

clarifying_info.q: What does the cost structure look like?
clarifying_info.a: Variable costs: raw materials 60% (mostly latex, a commodity — client has maximized purchasing economies of scale), labor 20%, overhead 20%. Fixed costs: client has a plant in Malaysia, as do competitors.

clarifying_info.q: What makes surgical gloves harder to produce?
clarifying_info.a: They require two molds instead of one, the fingertips need to be bent, sterilization is a bigger issue, and thickness is higher.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's sales and distribution situation?
clarifying_info.a: The client sells to all major hospitals in the US and has reasonably far-reaching international operations. It has good relationships with these hospitals. Hospitals also need many other accessories: gowns, tablecloths, masks, needles, scissors, etc.

exhibits.title: Segment overview table
exhibits.shows: A table with four columns (Segment, Q, P, Client MS%, Gross margin) comparing the exam glove and surgical glove segments

framework: Define the measure for shareholder value (e.g. profit/ROIC) and list factors that drive it
Prioritize segments by calculating current profit in each segment before diving deeper
Analyze the surgical glove segment: identify why growth lags competitors despite dominant share
Analyze the exam glove segment: identify why margins are being squeezed and whether new growth vectors are accessible
Develop recommendations for each segment to improve growth and/or profitability
Address cross-cutting levers: cost structure, distribution, and product innovation

questions.prompt: Calculate the current annual profit (gross profit) generated by each segment for the client.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use revenue = Q * P * market share, then apply gross margin. The surgical segment generates far more profit, so it should receive the most strategic attention.

math.setup: Segment profit = Market size (Q) * Price (P) * Client market share * Gross margin. Exam gloves: 1B units * $0.05 * 30% * 30%. Surgical gloves: 200M pairs * $0.50 * 50% * 50%.
math.answer: Exam gloves: ~$4.5M gross profit. Surgical gloves: ~$25M gross profit. Surgical segment is ~5.5x more profitable; it must be the primary focus.

questions.prompt: Why is the client growing more slowly than competitors in the surgical glove segment despite being the market leader with 50% share?
questions.guidance: Strong answer: client is not leveraging its dominant position and good hospital relationships. Competitors (B and C) are growing faster, suggesting product differentiation or distribution gaps. Key insight: unmet surgeon needs (e.g. thickness for bone surgeons) represent a product innovation opportunity. Candidate should probe unmet needs and cross-sell opportunities.

questions.prompt: Why is the client's profitability being squeezed in the exam glove segment?
questions.guidance: Strong answer: 15-20 competitors with many new entrants are driving price competition. The client's 30% market share makes it the leader, but pricing pressure is structural. The client is also missing the 7-8% growth coming from non-hospital segments (police, fire departments). Cost structure is largely fixed relative to competitors (all produce in Malaysia, latex is a commodity), so margin recovery requires either pricing power or volume in new segments.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific recommendations would you make to improve shareholder value across both segments?

categories.name: Surgical gloves — product innovation
ideas: Survey surgeons to identify unmet needs (e.g. thickness, fit, texture for specific specialties)
Develop thicker gloves for bone surgeons to eliminate need to stack 3-4 pairs
Introduce product line extensions targeted at specialty surgical needs
Use dominant market position and hospital relationships to pilot new products quickly

categories.name: Surgical gloves — cross-sell / diversification
ideas: Leverage existing hospital relationships to cross-sell related accessories: masks, gowns, tablecloths, needles, scissors
Form strategic alliance with or acquire manufacturers of high-margin hospital accessories
Become a one-stop shop for hospital consumables to increase wallet share and switching costs

categories.name: Surgical gloves — diversification trade-offs
ideas: Management attention and bandwidth risk with new product categories
Organizational complexity from SKU proliferation and cost-accounting challenges
Potential dilution of core competency in glove manufacturing

categories.name: Exam gloves — new growth segments
ideas: Sell to police departments and fire departments through established distribution channels
Target other non-hospital segments adopting safety standards requiring disposable gloves
Assess whether existing sales force can cover new segments or whether new channels are needed

categories.name: Exam gloves — manufacturing / cost
ideas: Consider outsourcing exam glove manufacturing to free up management attention for higher-profit surgical business
Outsourcing may also reduce manufacturing costs if a lower-cost contract manufacturer can be found
Evaluate whether exam gloves merit continued capital investment vs. managed-harvest approach

recommendation: Prioritize the surgical glove segment, which generates ~$25M gross profit (vs. ~$4.5M for exam gloves), by launching product innovation (specialty gloves for bone and other surgeons) and cross-selling hospital accessories to existing customers
In the exam glove segment, enter new growth segments (police, fire departments) using existing distribution channels to capture 7-8% market growth without building new infrastructure
Consider outsourcing exam glove manufacturing to reduce costs and redirect management focus to the higher-value surgical business
risks: Diversification into new hospital accessories (gowns, masks) carries execution risk and management distraction
New customer segments (police/fire) may have different procurement processes and price sensitivity than hospitals
Outsourcing exam gloves risks losing operational control and quality oversight
Competitors B and C may respond to product innovation with their own investments
next_steps: Commission surgeon needs survey to identify specific product gaps (e.g. thickness for bone surgeons)
Quantify the addressable market among non-hospital buyers (police, fire departments)
Evaluate build vs. buy vs. partner options for expanding into hospital accessories
Assess feasibility and cost savings of outsourcing exam glove manufacturing
